summary:
Elazığ province stands under the national framework of Turkey, where homosexuality has been decriminalised since 1858 and legal gender recognition has been available since 1988, and where discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited. That protection sits alongside a conspicuous absence of recognition: same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions and same-sex adoption have no legal standing, and LGBTI people are barred from serving openly in the military.

The direction of travel is restrictive. A leaked omnibus draft law, the 11th Judicial Package dated 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with sentences of up to three years. The same package would sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare by setting a minimum age of 25 and imposing onerous eligibility conditions, and would permit criminal charges against trans people and against the professionals who treat them. The government's stated justification is the protection of "the family" and "public morals". The package had not been enacted as reported; in early 2026 the government was separately considering criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality".

Local political conditions in Elazığ province are documented rather than inferred. On 19 December 2022 an anti-LGBT hate rally was held at Cumhuriyet (Republic) Square under the banner "LGBT sapkınlıktır" ("LGBT is perversion"), with the ruling AKP's deputy mayor Nazif Bilginoğlu in attendance. The rally statement condemned consensual same-sex relationships and same-sex marriage as a "revolting loss of reason" attributed to Western states, used the terms "perverse" and "degenerate mentality", and tied its gender and sexual themes to Turkey's denunciation of an international convention. State-facilitated, locally organised anti-LGBT mobilisation of this kind is the environment a visibly LGBTQ visitor enters.

Elsewhere in Turkey, and therefore as a reference point for what provincial policing can look like, authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches since 2015 using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Turkey 47th of 49, ahead only of Azerbaijan and Russia. Elazığ province inherits that standing without any local mechanism that would improve on it.

The 11th Judicial Package is a legislative vehicle carrying measures unrelated to gender and sexuality, including longer sentences for children and provisions for online-content removal. Provisions travelling inside a broader crime-and-punishment bill may attract less scrutiny than a standalone statute, and the package's reported status as a leak means its final form was not settled at the time of reporting.

The Elazığ rally's own language borrowed directly from the government's stated position on the Istanbul Convention, which shows local mobilisation and national rhetoric operating on the same vocabulary rather than as separate phenomena.
localsOnly:
Residents of Elazığ province face the same recognition gap as LGBT people nationwide: no legal status for same-sex partnership, no joint adoption, and no option to serve openly in the armed forces, despite the statutory prohibition on discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

Legal gender recognition has existed in Turkey since 1988, but the pending draft package would raise the age threshold for gender-affirming care to 25 and add eligibility conditions that residents would have to satisfy through the health system.

The presence of a serving AKP deputy mayor at the 2022 Cumhuriyet Square rally indicates that hostility in this province has been carried by elected officials from the governing party, which bears directly on how residents who are visibly LGBT are treated by local administration and by those who take their cue from it.

Residents also share the national pattern of Pride suppression: marches have been banned and broken up with tear gas, water cannons and mass arrests since 2015.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Elazığ-specific enforcement record appears in the inventory: there is no sourced count of police stops, GBT-style identity checks, detentions, prosecutions or hate-crime cases in the province, and no sourcing on how local police have treated trans visitors or residents. The 2022 rally is the only documented local event of its kind in the material provided.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted, amended or withdrawn after the reporting period of October 2025 is unresolved here, as is whether any provision of it was applied in Elazığ.

The claim that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited is carried by a general reference work rather than by a citation to a specific Turkish statute or article; the operative provision is not identified in the inventory.

Elazığ-specific data on healthcare access, the local availability of legal gender recognition paperwork, and the treatment of trans prisoners transferred from the province could not be sourced and should be treated as unresolved rather than as absent.
